title: What is prenatal physiotherapy, and when might I need it?
seoTitle: What prenatal physiotherapy covers in pregnancy
description: Prenatal physiotherapy assesses pregnancy pain, pelvic symptoms and movement limits. How it differs from a fitness class and when obstetric care comes first.
directAnswer: Prenatal physiotherapy is a clinical physiotherapy service for pregnancy-related movement problems, pelvic girdle or back pain, pelvic-floor symptoms and physical preparation for birth and early parenting tasks. It starts with history and examination, then a plan you agree together. It does not replace antenatal checks, scans or obstetric decisions. A general fitness or Pilates class can support activity when you are well, but it is not the same product as an individual pelvic-health assessment.

sections.heading: Concerns a pregnancy physiotherapist can discuss
paragraphs: Pelvic, Obstetric and Gynaecological Physiotherapy (POGP) describes specialist pelvic-health physiotherapists as clinicians with particular interest in pregnancy-related musculoskeletal pain, bladder and bowel continence symptoms and pelvic-related pain. A first visit usually maps the timeline of discomfort, which movements flare or settle it, earlier investigations or treatment, general health, and work or hobby demands.

Common reasons to book include pubic or sacroiliac pain on stairs or turning in bed, activity-related backache, heaviness or leakage with coughing, abdominal-wall concerns, and questions about pacing walking or lifting as the bump grows. Our guides to pelvic girdle pain and pregnancy backache explain those symptom patterns in more depth.

Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) works within physiotherapy scope: graded exercise, movement coaching, manual techniques when appropriate, and advice on supports such as belts when indicated. She does not diagnose obstetric complications or prescribe medicines.

sections.heading: How this differs from a general fitness class
paragraphs: A prenatal physio appointment is a private clinical assessment with a plan matched to your findings. A mixed-level fitness or Pilates class is coached movement for a group; even when the instructor is a physiotherapist, the hour is rarely a full medical work-up of every participant.

POGP notes that after assessment the physiotherapist discusses findings and options so you can plan treatment together. That may include pelvic-floor or trunk exercises, pacing advice, manual therapy, or referral back to a GP or maternity clinician if the problem does not look like ordinary pregnancy musculoskeletal pain.

If your main goal is general fitness in an uncomplicated pregnancy, a suitable prenatal class may be enough. If pain, leakage or instability is limiting daily tasks, assessment first usually saves trial-and-error in a busy class. Our STOTT Pilates overview explains method and Mat versus Reformer formats separately.

sections.heading: What to bring and what consent can include
paragraphs: Bring your maternity notes summary if you have one, any written activity limits from your obstetric team, a brief symptom timeline, and footwear you actually walk in. For bladder symptoms, POGP mentions that a short bladder diary can help planning; you will be told if that is useful for you.

For pregnancy-related pelvic or back pain, assessment often looks at how the back, hips and pelvis move and how the abdominal muscles activate, with your agreement. For bladder, bowel or persistent pelvic pain, an internal pelvic-floor examination may be offered. POGP states this is only with consent, that you may ask for a chaperone or bring a support person, and that you can decline and still receive help that does not require that exam.
Say in advance if online video feels more comfortable for the first conversation, or if you prefer in-person hands-on care in Bangalore or Ahmedabad.

sections.heading: When obstetric or emergency care comes first
paragraphs: Physiotherapy does not replace midwifery or obstetric review for bleeding, reduced baby movements, suspected waters breaking, regular painful contractions, fever with pelvic pain, severe headache with visual change, or sudden chest pain and breathlessness. Those need maternity triage or emergency services (112 in India), not a routine physio slot.

If the physiotherapist suspects the problem is not pregnancy-related pelvic girdle or back pain, POGP advice is that they may suggest you see another clinician such as your GP. Follow that escalation rather than booking more classes.

sections.heading: Online sessions versus in-person care
paragraphs: Video sessions can cover history, movement screening you can do in camera view, education, and exercise progression when you are medically stable. Hands-on joint or soft-tissue treatment, belt fitting and some pelvic-floor examinations need an in-person visit.

Choose the format that matches the question you need answered. Many people start online for advice on pacing and exercise, then attend in person if pain or pelvic-floor assessment requires it. Either way, keep your maternity team informed about new red-flag symptoms.

faqs.question: Is prenatal physiotherapy only for people in pain?
faqs.answer: No. Pain and pelvic-floor symptoms are common reasons to attend, but you can also ask about pacing activity, preparing for birth positions, or returning to movement after pregnancy complications once your maternity clinician agrees exercise is suitable.

faqs.question: Do I need a doctor’s referral?
faqs.answer: Pathways vary. In many places you can book a women’s health physiotherapist directly, while hospital services may need a midwife or doctor referral. Bring any obstetric limits to the visit either way.
